title: India-UK Trade Deal Takes Effect as First Zero-Duty Shipments Leave Indian Ports
excerpt: Exports worth $140 million shipped on Day One under the new CETA agreement, which eliminates tariffs on 99% of Indian goods entering Britain and opens 137 services sub-sectors.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India exported $140 million in duty-free goods to the UK on the first day of CETA.
  • Britain eliminated tariffs on 96.8% of its tariff lines, covering 97.7% of trade value.
  • Over 75,000 Indian professionals benefit from social security exemptions for up to five years.
  • Bilateral trade is projected to reach $100–120 billion, doubling from $55–56 billion.

  • India shipped $140 million in duty-free exports to the UK on July 15, the first day of the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
  • Britain eliminated tariffs on 96.8% of tariff lines immediately, covering 97.7% of bilateral trade by value.
  • The accompanying Double Contribution Convention exempts over 75,000 Indian professionals from dual social security payments for up to five years.
  • Both governments project bilateral trade will reach $100–120 billion, roughly doubling from the current $55–56 billion.

India and the United Kingdom's Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement came into force on July 15, and Indian exporters wasted no time putting it to work. Consignments worth approximately $140 million — spanning textiles, gems and jewellery, leather, footwear, and engineering goods — left ports across the country on Day One under zero-duty terms, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said at an event organised by the Commerce Department.

What the Deal Covers

Under the agreement, signed in London in July 2025 after 14 rounds of negotiations stretching back to 2021, Britain removed duties on 96.8% of its tariff lines immediately, covering 97.7% of bilateral trade by value. India eliminated tariffs on 64.1% of lines at once and will phase out duties on a further 21%, while shielding sensitive agricultural categories such as dairy, millets, and edible oils.

The tariff cuts are sweeping. Duties as high as 70% on processed foods, over 21% on marine products, around 18% on engineering goods and auto components, up to 16% on leather and footwear, and about 12% on textiles have all been reduced to zero for Indian exporters.

"The FTA is not the ceiling; it's the floor of our ambitions. We are seeing Vision 2030 as a much wider partnership between the UK and India."

- Lindy Cameron, UK High Commissioner to India

Jewellery, Engineering Among Big Winners

The gems and jewellery sector stands to gain substantially. The Gem & Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC) projects that Indian exports to the UK in this sector could more than triple — from $754 million currently to $2.5 billion — over the coming years. GJEPC Chairman Kirit Bhansali said the zero-duty access would enhance the attractiveness of Indian products across key segments, including diamond jewellery, coloured gemstone jewellery, silver jewellery, and lab-grown diamond jewellery.

Engineering exports are another growth area. Britain is already among India's top five markets for engineering goods, with shipments reaching $4.7 billion in fiscal year 2025/26. EEPC India Chairman Pankaj Chadha said the agreement could help push that figure beyond $7.5 billion by 2029/30.

Services and Professional Mobility

The deal goes beyond goods. It opens 137 services sub-sectors to Indian firms, covering IT, financial services, education, consulting, telecommunications, and engineering. Mobility provisions for business visitors, intra-company transferees, and independent professionals have been simplified.

In a first for India, the agreement establishes annual quotas for 1,800 Indian chefs, yoga instructors, and classical musicians to work in the UK.

The accompanying Double Contribution Convention, which also took effect on July 15, addresses a long-standing pain point for the diaspora workforce. Eligible Indian professionals on temporary UK assignments — and their employers — are now exempt from paying into both India's and Britain's social security systems simultaneously, for up to five years. The government estimates this will benefit more than 75,000 workers and over 900 companies.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly 1.9 million people of Indian origin in the UK, the trade deal has direct implications. The social security relief reduces the cost of deploying Indian talent to Britain, a move that could increase hiring across IT firms and consultancies. Cheaper Indian textiles, jewellery, and processed foods entering the UK duty-free could also show up in retail pricing, though the timeline for consumer impact remains unclear.

On the other side, Indian consumers stand to pay less for Scotch whisky, luxury British automobiles — including Jaguar Land Rover and Rolls-Royce under a quota system that could cut prices by 20–30% — and British cosmetics and fashion goods.

What Comes Next

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal called the deal a "defining milestone in India-UK ties" and said it unlocked fresh avenues for MSMEs, farmers, and manufacturers. The Commerce Department said it would work with Export Promotion Councils and industry clusters to maximise utilisation of the pact's provisions.

The agreement also opens Britain's £90 billion ($121 billion) government procurement market to Indian suppliers for the first time. India has offered reciprocal procurement access worth about $14 billion.

One unresolved issue is the UK's proposed Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which could affect Indian exports if implemented next year. Officials said discussions were ongoing.

Both countries have set a target of reaching $120 billion in bilateral trade by 2030–31, roughly doubling the current $56 billion. Whether the CETA becomes the springboard for that ambition will depend on how quickly Indian exporters — from Tiruppur's garment makers to Surat's jewellers — adapt to the new rules of origin and documentation requirements.

Sector Gains from Zero-Duty Access
›Gems and jewellery exports projected to triple to $2.5 billion.
›Engineering exports expected to exceed $7.5 billion by 2029.
›137 services sub-sectors opened for Indian firms.
›Annual quotas for 1,800 Indian professionals established.
